title: The sick first (ch. 36)
hook: care of the sick is placed above all

segments.voice: Yesterday, tools as altar vessels: the saucepan handled like the chalice. Your line was everything is holy.

Before all things, and above all things. Strong words for any rule to use, and Saint Benedict doesn't spend them lightly. Earlier this week the Rule said nothing is to be put before the work of God. So what could come before all things? Not the abbot. Not the chapel. Not the harvest or the library. Chapter thirty-six answers in its first line, and the answer is the brother lying in the infirmary with a fever.
screen: `BEFORE ALL THINGS, ABOVE ALL THINGS.` → `WHAT COULD COME BEFORE EVERYTHING?` → `THE BROTHER WITH A FEVER.`

segments.voice: Benedict writes that care of the sick must come before all things and above all things, so that they are served as Christ himself. He gives Christ's words from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me," and "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." One way to hold the two "before" lines together: the work of God comes first, and the sick are served as Christ. The same Christ, in the chapel and in the sickbed. Then Benedict gets specific. The sick get their own room, and a brother to look after them who is God-fearing, careful and attentive. They may have baths as often as it helps them. The very weak may eat meat, normally kept off the monks' table, to get their strength back; when they recover, they go back to the usual fare. The abbot takes the greatest care that the sick suffer no neglect, and checks that the cellarer and attendants let nothing slip. Here's the part that keeps it honest. Benedict speaks to the sick, too. They should remember they're served for the honor of God, and not wear out their brothers with unreasonable demands. Then, in the very next breath, he tells the brothers: bear with them patiently anyway, because from such as these a greater reward is gained. Patience is asked of both sides of the bed. Nobody in this chapter is a saint already. They're just people being asked to carry each other.
screen: `THE SICK: BEFORE ALL, ABOVE ALL.` · `SERVED AS CHRIST HIMSELF.` · `A ROOM, A CAREFUL NURSE, BATHS, MEAT.` · `PATIENCE ON BOTH SIDES OF THE BED.` · then, large: `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is sick right now, in the hospital, at home with a long illness, or worn down by something nobody sees, and hold their face in your mind for a few breaths, along with one small kindness that might reach them: a visit, a call, a meal left at the door. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, keep them in mind a little longer, kindly.
The sick first. In Benedict's Rule, care of the sick comes before all things and above all things, because they are served as Christ. Today's word.
Your line: before all things. In the chapel and at the sickbed, the same Christ is served. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities care for their sick and elderly members within the monastery, and Catholics count visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy drawn from Matthew 25.

chat.says: What does Benedict's Rule say must come before all things and above all things?
options: Care of the sick, because they're served as Christ himself: sick, and you visited me.
The harvest, since the whole monastery depends on it to feed the sick and poor.
The abbot's orders, since he holds the place of Christ in the monastery.
chat.meaning: Chapter thirty-six puts care of the sick before and above all things, serving them as Christ, with patience asked of both sick and carers.

notes: Editor pass: the reconciliation of chapter 36 with chapter 43 is now offered as one way to read them, not as the narrator's ruling.

The Rule is paraphrased. Check the summary of ch. 36: 'Infirmorum cura ante omnia et super omnia adhibenda est', served as Christ; Matthew 25:36 and 25:40; the sick not to distress the brothers by superfluous demands, yet to be borne patiently, since from such a greater reward is gained; the abbot's great care that they suffer no neglect; a separate cell and a God-fearing, diligent, careful attendant; baths as often as expedient; meat for the very weak, given up on recovery; the abbot to see that cellarer and attendants do not neglect them.

The reconciliation of ch. 36 ('before all things') with ch. 43 ('nothing before the work of God') as 'the same Christ, in the chapel and in the sickbed' is the script's own reading, not the Rule's; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
'meat, normally kept off the monks' table' refers to the Rule's restriction on the flesh of four-footed animals (ch. 39); confirm the simplified phrasing.
howItsDone: visiting the sick as one of the corporal works of mercy; confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Matthew 25:36 and 25:40.
